member of the commission. − i will perhaps start with the second point. i think we need to be aware, from the debate on oil, that we could face a similar situation with an unpredictable growth in demand in other sectors, and food is the one that is a really basic need for people. so we need technology to give us a broader opportunity. broader opportunity definitely comes when you use things that usually just go to waste. so for this purpose i believe that we clearly need to promote second-generation. i would say that perhaps even this is not sufficient, because there we do not have the risks. we need new technologies. it is not just that we would like to replace oil with biofuels, but that we have technology that really guarantees that we do not have this competition, or limited competition. that is why – even if in theory all technologies should be equal – i still believe that the second generation is worthy of particular attention. with regard to education, i believe that this is a broader part of education. there are educational programmes, because generally this is not education about biofuels but about sustainability, energy efficiency and a quite different attitude towards the environment and knowing that whatever you use is taken from somewhere and is always doing damage. sometimes, in the debate on biofuels, we forget that oil is also produced and sometimes it is produced from tar sands. recently some pictures have been published about where it is produced. it is not a farm and it is really also a challenge. so i believe that each of us, when using energy, should try to use it as efficiently as possible and follow the trend of using greener energy, supporting this even it if it costs a bit more.
member of the commission. − the commission recognises that there is greater demand in the european union for biodiesel as a replacement for diesel fuel rather than bioethanol, which could reduce petrol consumption. with this in mind it can be expected that in the years to come biodiesel consumption in the eu will remain higher than that of bioethanol. nevertheless, the commission believes that it is not necessary to have technologically specific targets as both biodiesel and bioethanol can have an important role to play in reducing the oil dependence of the european transport sector. having said this, it is second-generation which promotes biodiesel or bioethanol independently, but still demand in the eu market is definitely bigger for diesel. i do not believe that we should discriminate between ethanol and diesel, but we should encourage second-generation instead of first-generation.
member of the commission. − i would be in the 35% camp, because it is important that, if we put requirements that completely ban biofuels from the market and there is too high a risk of leverage, we will move to oil – and deeper – and perhaps to coal and liquid technology. in my opinion this is worse than really keeping 35% as the threshold, and a 35% threshold is clearly saving co2. so i will stay with 35%. it is now up to negotiations with parliament and council: if it comes to be a different figure, well, i will live with this figure, but i think 35% is rather tough, because in the college, when the figure was discussed, we were also in different camps, and this is already compromised from the two camps: one that believes in biofuels and one that is afraid of biofuels. so 35% was actually the compromise.
member of the commission. − we are very positive about the development of geothermal, and i believe that the draft directive now being discussed, and the climate-energy package, will facilitate the use of renewable power, including geothermal. why is it not being used now? well, partly because it is not sufficient to focus on the renewables. it is much easier to pass the costs of fossil fuels to the consumers, because to use renewable energy, like geothermal, you need capital investment, and for this you need a specific environment for, and focus on, renewables. so i believe that a renewable energy source, like geothermal, will have much better developments in the eu, not only for power production but, for example, in copenhagen it is used for district heating. so there are different applications of this technology, and it will grow in the european union. concerning energy content: it is true that biofuels have a low energy content and you need bigger volumes, and i think we should not be mistaken that we will replace oil with biofuels. but at least here i drive a car that is powered by biofuel, and its only disadvantage is that i need to go to a service station much more often, but i do not mind this. that is why i would say that it is different, but not so different as to make me change my behaviour. that will be a problem with the electric car. at the moment it is very much slower, at least at this stage – city-run cars. perhaps there is a need for some kind of hybrid, because if you travel a longer distance, electric vehicles might not be satisfactory – but for biofuel-driven vehicles there is no problem.
member of the commission. − you know that the commission yesterday decided on a proposal for the second roaming package − this time on sms and data roaming. parliament will remember very well that this analysis of the market was done at the request of parliament which, during the voice roaming package in june last year, put in article 11 of the regulation that the commission should come back to sms and data roaming in due course in 2008. that is what the commission did, and you know that we have proposed price caps. that brings me to the question of price fixing. no, we do not fix prices. we fix ceilings under which operators have the flexibility to compete and to innovate, either with roaming offers below the maximum oral tariff ceilings or with other packages which customers might then chose. so, flexibility is given. as regards sms, the evidence suggests that prices have been more or less static over the last year and remain at levels that cannot be justified by reference to the underlying cost, and the sms market presents roughly the same problems as the market in voice roaming. in february this year, i went to the gsm association world congress in barcelona and warned the industry. i spoke personally with industry leaders to tell them that they had time to bring down prices by themselves and that the deadline was 1 july. what we saw is that the prices between last year and this year for sms roaming did not move at all. our proposal therefore is to cap the retail charge at a maximum of 11 cents and the wholesale charge at a maximum of 4 cents. turning to data roaming, we have included actions to deal with the very famous cases of bill shocks where customers have to pay several thousand euros when they come back from one or two weeks abroad, because they used their mobile phone for data downloading in the same way as at home where a data download per megabyte could cost between 5 and 15 cents. abroad, it can go up to 16 euros per megabyte so you can imagine what kind of bills you can receive if you are now aware of what is happening. that is why we have proposed several measures. the first is a transparency measure to inform citizens crossing a border what data roaming will cost. the second is a measure where the consumer can fix, together with his operator, a ceiling over which he does not want to pay any more so that communications are then cut; and the third is because we have seen that the whole problem here comes from highly overpriced wholesale costs which one operator imposes on another. that is why we propose a wholesale cap at one euro per megabyte, hoping that normal price structures can then be developed and offered to consumers.

president of the council. - madam president, mr president of the european commission, ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament, as you will readily understand, after the moment of emotion, humanity and solidarity we have just experienced with the testimony and arrest of ingrid betancourt, it is difficult to speak before your assembly. but we must face up to the facts. the european council meets on 15 and 16 october. this new session is of particular importance at a time of crisis and instability which calls for the european union to show political will, take initiatives and take decisions. the economic and financial situation will dominate the work of the european council. as i said to you on 23 september, this crisis is not a purely american crisis. this is a european crisis today. it's now an international crisis. the crisis of confidence in the markets and in our financial sector has worsened in recent days. the union must take its responsibilities. the presidency of the council is determined to spare no effort to increase the coordination and coherence of national initiatives. it did so on saturday with the meeting of the european members of the g7, in the presence of the president of the european commission, the president of the eurogroup and the president of the european central bank. it did so yesterday at the meeting of the council of ministers for economic and financial affairs. it will do so again at the european council on 15 and 16 october. we have reached agreement among europeans on the need for close consultation on the management by each member state of the effects of the crisis on its own financial system. european concertation is a reality. there are constant contacts between governments, administrations, central banks, banking supervisors and the european commission. as jean-claude trichet has said, we are responding to the crisis with our own resources and structures. we are not a federal state like the united states of america. we have nothing to be ashamed of, we have to deal with the institutional context that is ours. it's time to move. the key is that europeans act together and take responsibility alongside the european central bank. in his statement of monday 6 october, the president of the european council, nicolas sarkozy, reiterated the unanimous will of the european union's leaders to take all the necessary measures to ensure the stability of the financial system. we must welcome the role played by the european central bank and the other central banks - the us, the uk, sweden, switzerland and canada - which have just decided to cut interest rates by half a percentage point. we must continue to act without delay. as the finance ministers said at their meeting yesterday, there is an urgent need to reassure depositors and to provide a liquidity boost to the interbank market. that's how we'll restore trust. we also need to make a major overhaul of financial governance in a direction more favourable to the long-term financing of the economy, to the mobilisation of europeans' savings, and to a reduction in financial volatility and speculation. all this is not incompatible with maintaining a competitive and innovative financial industry. we are relying heavily on the proposals of the european commission to improve this governance. they must be swift and bold. the member states agreed yesterday on an immediate response to ensure the stability of financial institutions by recapitalising them or by any other means required by the circumstances. in this respect, the guidelines announced this morning by the british prime minister are welcome. they are clearly in line with the commitments made by the heads of state or government on 6 october. france, for its part, envisages a legal structure allowing the state to take, where appropriate, financial contributions when and where necessary. the president of the european council will continue to build on these various initiatives and proposals to take appropriate initiatives to strengthen european coordination. we must also safeguard and guarantee the interests of depositors. the minimum level of deposit protection in europe is to be raised, as you know, to 50,000 euros. some member states, and many of them, have announced their decision to raise this protection to eur 100 000. in the present exceptional circumstances, flexibility in the application of the community state aid rules and the provisions of the stability and growth pact is necessary. the european commission, under the decisive impulse of its president, is helping us in this very particular case. international coordination at the g7 meeting this weekend is also needed to restore confidence. as the japanese finance minister, the current chairman of the g7, has said, the g7 must send a strong message, jointly from the finance ministers and central bank governors. that is what the central banks have just done and it is a decisive and very positive signal from this point of view. we must perhaps involve the major emerging countries in stabilising the markets, given the international nature of this crisis. this is the whole point of the enlarged g8 which the president of the european council has called for by the end of the year. finally, the international monetary fund must be the main forum for discussion between the major players in the world. it must regain the role of financial policeman that it had originally and, as was foreseen in the aftermath of the second world war, it must be concerned with monetary and financial stability, and not merely with monitoring the situation in the emerging or developing countries. beyond these extremely important developments on the economic and financial crisis, the council presidency wished that the council could discuss the climate/energy package. under the decisive impetus of the german presidency, the european council in march 2007 made ambitious commitments on the environment. we want to preserve this environmental ambition of the package presented by the commission, on which we want, i say clearly, agreement with your assembly at first reading. we must be ready and in a strong position for the two meetings in poznań in december 2008 and in copenhagen at the end of 2009. however, the current economic downturn is likely to exacerbate the concerns of some of our partners and our industries. we must, together, address these concerns. we must look for the flexibilities we can provide without, however, calling into question the objectives, the fundamentals and the broad balances of the package proposed by the commission, because what is at issue in this package is the development model we will have to manage tomorrow, a development model mr president, the turco decision is an important legal and democratic step. it tells us that the concept of public interest contained in regulation no 1049/01, which defines citizens' access to documents, must be interpreted in such a way that the right to a wider knowledge of the facts which led to the adoption of a decision is considered more important and takes precedence over the safeguarding of the internal procedure by which the decision was taken. the turco decision tells us that it is important for citizens to know - they have a right to know - not only how the decision was made, not only the reasons for it, but also the documents on which it was based so that their knowledge is as broad as possible. the commission has already taken the necessary steps to ensure that the council and the commission are able to take account of the decisions of the european parliament and the council of ministers, and to ensure that the council and the commission are able to take account of the decisions of the council and the commission. there are, of course, perhaps some problems with the so-called confidentiality of documents, especially with regard to the opinions of the legal service. i'm a lawyer and i know it! but that should in no way lead us to say that these documents should remain secret because they can lead to some problems. i think it should lead us to say that the whole culture of transparency must change. transparency is balance, respect and in the process but not fear of knowledge. i'll close with one last observation: i think it is important to see here the difference between what is actually happening in the council and in parliament, in our institution. in parliament, access to both meetings and documents is almost complete. i think that with the turco decision it is possible to harmonize upwards for the council.

the remaining problematic issues have been completed. the negotiations that took place in july delivered some real progress. the emerging package outlined a possible balanced outcome which respected the european union’s key requirements in agriculture while delivering valuable benefits for our industrial manufacturers. a broad outline of the agreement has emerged on different key issues, including the overall reduction in trade-distorting domestic support in the agricultural sector, the scope that developed and developing countries would retain to shield a limited number of sensitive and special products from tariff cuts, the swiss formula used to determine tariff cuts for industrial products, and the flexibility to be made available to developing countries to shield a number of industrial products from those cuts. in the assessment made by the commission, this package contains real value for european business and consumers and would ensure an international legal framework for agriculture fully in line with the 2003 reform. in our opinion, the emerging package also contains real development value for the poorest countries in the world. a round concluded on this basis would reduce world tariffs by half and, while developing countries would contribute one-third of the savings, they would benefit from two-thirds of the increased market access. it would also ensure that oecd economies join europe’s initiative in providing least developed countries with duty free and quota free access to their markets – what we normally call our ‘everything but arms’ initiative. we would also have succeeded in locking in real farm reform in the united states. with an agreement, the united states would have had to reduce their trade-distorting domestic support or subsidies to usd 14.5 billion. without it, subsidies can now go up to usd 48 billion under the new farm bill. it would also serve our interests to get permanent international legal protection of our reformed common agricultural policy. a deal on this basis would turn the emerging countries into custodians of the multilateral trading system which needs to be preserved but also to be strengthened. we would anchor them more firmly into the rule-based system of global trade which is essential for the future. it was therefore a disappointment that it proved impossible to close the discussions on the doha modalities in july because of continuing disagreement on a very specific point in the agricultural field. the difficulties arose over the issue of special agricultural safeguards for developing countries, the so-called ssm, essentially within the g7 grouping. india and china were unable to agree with the united states over the triggers and the remedies to be put in place for this safeguard when it is used to breach pre-doha-round rates. since early september, contacts have been taking place at senior official level to try to resolve this continuing difference of views, but we have not yet been successful on this issue. though the european union remains firmly committed and engaged, it is actually unclear how far discussions will pick up in the coming weeks. as normal, we will maintain strong dialogue with parliament and we will of course hope for your continued support on this issue.

the rapporteur. - the mr president, the 29 european regulatory bodies are prima facie micro-institutions, but in fact they have obvious long-term effects and are already an accepted institutional component of the union. the excessive increase in the number of regulatory bodies has undoubtedly led to an expansion of european regulatory intervention, to the fragmentation and opacity of european policies and, consequently, to the difficulty of their functional coordination. the european organizations as a whole are urgently raising the question of an interim report on their work and performance. a minimum set of common principles and rules for the structure, operation and control of regulatory bodies is required in order to integrate them harmoniously into the framework of the fundamental principles deriving from the system of the treaties. following the council's refusal to accept a legally binding act and the rejection of the proposal to conclude an interinstitutional agreement, the commission decided to propose the setting up of an interinstitutional working party to develop a common framework for regulatory bodies and to define the responsibilities of each of the european institutions vis-à-vis those bodies. i think that this proposal falls short of the european parliament's expectations of an interinstitutional agreement. the common approach is indeed an intermediate step towards the adoption of a legally binding text. i understand the commission's desire to get out of a situation of prolonged institutional inertia. the establishment of an interinstitutional working group to take collective political stock of the experience gained from the activities of regulatory bodies and to clarify their position on multilevel european governance is welcome. the proposed approach to the structure and operation of these bodies is as close as possible to the common approach, with the aim of reducing red tape in order to achieve proper and effective regulatory intervention and supervision and to meet, at least in part, the audit and accountability requirements of the times. the priority of the common framework for interinstitutional coordination and convergence pursued is to maximise the added value of regulatory bodies to the overall european governance structures in terms of greater transparency, visible democratic control and enhanced efficiency. finally, i would like to emphasize that the introduction of parliamentary control over the structure and work of the regulatory bodies is in keeping with the classic democratic principle which requires the development of political responsibility for each body of executive authority. the possibility for the european parliament to attribute political responsibility to these bodies is linked to the core of representative democracy to examine the options of the executive from the point of view of legality and expediency.

in writing. at the same time that the centre-right and centre-left governments of its member states refuse to meet the slightest wage or other demand of the workers, citing the resilience of the economy, the european council is provocatively financing the banks and monopolies with trillions of euros, again putting the burden of the crisis on the backs of the workers. the acceleration of capitalist restructuring, the dismantling of industrial relations, the dismantling of social protection and insurance systems, the linking of wages to competitiveness and employment are at the heart of the new wave of eu summit decisions. the european pact on migration and asylum, which erects inhuman walls for migrants in the eu, but provides the necessary cheap labour for the monopolies, complements the savage attack. at the same time, the council decisions reveal the eu's hypocritical concern for the climate, since the price of energy will now be formed on the basis of a market gamble, regardless of its production costs, thus increasing the profits of monopolies and burdening the environment. there can be no pro-people solutions in the context of competitiveness and the liberalised action of capital, which the eu and governments are further reinforcing with measures of a state monopoly nature, while escalating the anti-people offensive to bring the capitalist system out of its crisis.
in writing. the directive, which was voted for by the european parliament, establishes the functioning and activities of temporary employment agencies, which it calls by the misleading title of 'temporary employment agencies', under the pretext of guaranteeing workers' supposedly 'equal rights'. it requires the member states to prohibit any obstacle to their establishment and action and guarantees their right to be paid for their 'services', i.e. ransom for the slave trade. in fact, it relieves the real employer of any obligation to the workers, who are considered employees of the slave-trading company-phantom, which only on paper employs staff. employers can thus be exempted from compliance with obligations imposed by labour and insurance legislation (e.g. insurance contributions) and from any liability, such as compensation for work accidents. in fact, the directive does not guarantee rights for workers who are victims of trafficking, but rather exempts them from those rights. the so-called safeguarding of workers' rights turns out to be the safeguarding of slave companies, the legalization of capital's insolvency, the savage exploitation of the working class. the satisfaction of the modern popular needs and rights presupposes the overthrow of the anti-working class policy of the eu, the workers' counter-attack, which will shape the conditions for the people's alliance, to claim their own people's power.
in writing. the promotion of clean and energy-efficient road transport vehicles is, from a technical point of view, an essential measure for environmental protection, because emissions from conventional vehicles contribute to climate change and to the air pollution of urban centres with serious effects on public health. despite the mobilization of workers to address these serious problems, the car manufacturers, in the context of competition, refuse to proceed with the production of 'clean cars' unless their even greater profitability is first ensured, requiring the costs of research and applications for clean cars to be financed, along with their increased profits, by the state. the proposed directive does just that by making it compulsory to take into account, in the public procurement criteria for vehicles, the operating costs of energy consumption, co2 emissions and pollutant emissions throughout the life of vehicles, thus provoking subsidies to the car industry to produce cleaner vehicles with public money. the workers are fighting for public transport organisations which will provide them with quality and genuinely environmentally friendly services. they oppose all kinds of regulations designed to enrich the car industry, which, by its unfair social and environmental attitude, in order to increase its profits, contributes to the phenomenon of climate change, to the overconsumption of energy resources, and to air pollution.
in writing. the right of workers to rest and holidays has been turned into a commodity that enriches capital. time-sharing leases and the new products promoted in this context take advantage of the continuing reduction in holiday time, the squeeze on incomes and the effort of workers to secure cheaper holidays in the long term, generating turnover of over eur 11 billion. the fraudulent and aggressive methods used by companies, often ghost companies, to convince and deceive buyers start at best with the fine print of contracts, misleading advertising, tedious presentations, promises of gifts, etc., and almost always end with the immediate and pressing signing of binding documents. the complaints that reach consumer organizations about fraud, excessive maintenance costs, credit card issues, significant price reductions at resale due to marketing expenses, etc., are endless. the inclusion of other products in the time-based credit directive, such as holidays on boats, clubs and caravans, provides legal cover and new profits for the activities of the capital. the right of withdrawal limited to 10 days and subject to a fine of 3% of the total amount does not solve the problem. instead, the eu is shifting the responsibility onto the backs of workers as it does with all consumer products.

member of the commission. −madam president, may i take the liberty of answering mr ryan’s comments very briefly? i just want to tell you that you will soon receive a full, legally based answer from the head of my cabinet office. then you will understand our position. concerning the second issue, customs cooperation is an important part of the eu-china strategic partnership. the ec-china agreement on customs cooperation and mutual administrative assistance with china provides the legal basis for this cooperation. the ec-china joint customs cooperation committee meets once a year in order to manage and oversee the implementation of the agreement. under the customs cooperation agreement, the ec and china are developing substantial interaction in key customs areas, organised clearly to reflect the interest of the european community. the problem of counterfeiting is our key priority in relation to china, which is the number one source of fakes entering the eu external borders. during my visits to beijing in january and april 2008, i agreed with my chinese counterparts to develop an ambitious action plan for ipr enforcement with concrete objectives and measures to be adopted by the eu-china summit in december. it should include, among other things, an information exchange system on ipr risks, an exchange programme of operational officials, and collaboration on the development of partnerships with business communities in china and the european union. securing the supply chain is another essential aspect of ec-china customs cooperation. the joint pilot project on safe and secure trade lane has been running since november 2007 with the participation of three ports, shenzhen in china, rotterdam in the netherlands and felixstowe in the united kingdom. this project aims at strengthening security while facilitating trade between the ec and china through the use of modern technology and the exchange of advance information. at the same time, it will help to better target the traffic in illicit goods. furthermore, the pilot project aims at preparing the ground for a future agreement on mutual recognition of security measures and the authorised economic operator (aeo) and its chinese opposite number. it involves cooperation in such important fields as alignment of the chinese security legislation, information exchange and risk analysis. china has in the meantime adopted and implemented, as of 1 april 2008, its own aeo legislation that appears very similar to the european community concept. the ec and china are also enhancing cooperation in other important areas. an eu-china agreement on coordinated controls of trade in drug precursors is expected to be signed at the upcoming eu-china summit that will allow us to combat trade in illicit drugs more effectively. we agreed to further enhance our cooperation to fight fraud through the established mutual assistance mechanism. the european anti-fraud office (olaf) has posted one of its agents in china in order to support the anti-contraband and anti-counterfeit activities of the office, in particular in relation to cigarette smuggling. the eu is ready to continue to assist china in customs capacity building, including through the application of the recently published customs blueprints. while we have made considerable progress in enhancing customs cooperation with china, further steps need to be taken, particularly with regard to combating counterfeit and piracy. proper implementation of the above-mentioned initiatives, in particular the proposed ipr enforcement action plan, will determine the level of effectiveness of this cooperation.

president of the council. - madam president, i shall try to answer this set of questions relating to the financial crisis which has been affecting the world economy for more than 15 months and which continues to weigh on the financing of european economies. as regards the union, i would remind you that the council meeting of 15 and 16 october last confirmed the commitment that, in all circumstances, the necessary measures will be taken to safeguard the stability of the financial system, to support the important financial institutions, to prevent bankruptcies and to ensure the protection of savers' deposits. as regards the financial system, the european council also strongly called for accountability of all actors in the financial system, in particular the banking sector. he stressed that the real performance of company executives should be reflected in their pay, including severance pay and anything related to golden parachutes. similarly, it agreed to ensure that stock option profits or the remuneration system do not lead to excessive risk taking or an extreme focus on short-term objectives. following this meeting, the informal meeting of heads of state and government on 7 november to prepare the coordinated european approach to the g20 meeting held last weekend in washington aimed to take swift decisions on transparency, global regulatory standards, including accounting, financial supervision and crisis management, preventing conflicts of interest and creating an early warning system to build confidence for savers and investors. in particular, in reply to the question put to me by the honourable member on behalf of the pse, who took up mr evans' question, on the concrete measures under consideration to deal with the crisis, i would like to refer to the reform of the directive on bank capital requirements which is under consideration in the council. the council's work on this proposal is well advanced. the commission has also recently proposed a regulation on a system of accreditation of credit rating agencies. this proposal goes in the same direction, in that the capital requirements are determined on the basis of the ratings granted. as regards the protection of deposits by savers, the commission proposed amending the existing directive to increase the minimum guarantee to eur 50 000, with a view to a second increase to eur 100 000 in the future. the european parliament and the council are currently examining this proposal. i would also like to note that following the european council of 15 and 16 october, the financial crisis unit was set up. as you know, this unit is an informal mechanism for alerting, exchanging information and evaluating between the representatives of the council, the president of the european council, the commission, its president, the president of the european central bank, the president of the eurogroup and the governments of the member states, as well as, of course, the president of the economic and financial committee, who is the working head of this unit. in reply to the questions put by mrs mcguinness and mr mitchell, i would like to point out that the european member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all, i think the debate has shown that we all agree that we must act quickly, very quickly, in a tragic situation. as regards the sending of a european force to the east of the drc, i believe that it has become clear that only a european force whose sole purpose is to secure the humanitarian space could possibly be accepted by all the countries in the region. it would therefore be a question of imposing on all parties to the conflict a humanitarian ceasefire for the delivery of aid to the populations near the front. this is precisely what the great lakes countries are asking for, for whom a ceasefire and the delivery of humanitarian aid remain an absolute and immediate priority. in this connection, they also indicated the ways to be explored: political negotiation and, above all, as we all said, the strengthening of monuc. although the humanitarian situation is gradually coming under control, some member states do not seem to exclude the possibility of a cfsp mission. however, no final decision will be taken until there is european unanimity on this matter and the united nations security council formally decides on it. as regards the strengthening of monuc, i think it is absolutely essential, and so does louis michel. monuc is taking a constructive and objective approach to this conflict, but we cannot ask it to do anything that is not its mission. monuc must maintain peace within a certain agreed framework and not impose peace on all parties by military means. it's hard to grasp sometimes, but i think the nuance is quite considerable. however, it is clear that, given the size of the congo and the complexity of the problem, monuc is not sufficiently equipped - president of the council. - madam president, thank you to all the speakers, this is a very rich debate on an important subject and i share, like the presidency, the feeling expressed by the majority of you, that we must absolutely assume our responsibilities in dealing with an exceptional situation affecting a structuring industry: you mentioned the figures, 12 million jobs in the european union and an industry which is affected by the financial crisis, because of the share of consumer credit, which is the hallmark of this industry. it is also an industry facing unprecedented environmental challenges. it is one thing that we have fallen behind, but it is another that we do not have to catch up, at a time when we are also committed to the energy-climate package and this is one of the major challenges facing the european union. so the situation is exceptional and the european response, for the presidency, must be up to the challenge. this answer must take account of three factors: the first factor is what our partners in third countries are doing. the competitiveness of this european industry must be preserved. secondly, the major objectives of the european union must be preserved: the commission's proposals must help to achieve the objectives of the energy and climate package that you know; in writing. i voted against the capoulas santos report on the new support scheme for farmers under the common agricultural policy, as i believe that it is not possible to ensure the sustainability of agriculture at european level. indeed, financing the agricultural sector is essential to ensure the sustainability of the sector and food security in europe. however, this financing should be provided from the community budget and not be at the expense of the small and medium-sized producer, as for example by establishing minimum aid ceilings. on the contrary, the criterion of staff should be given great weight in the payment of aid and a maximum aid per holding should be established. the crisis management system proposed by the commission is also considered to be inadequate. it is more appropriate to set up a public insurance fund based on community funding, aimed at preventing crises and epidemics and ensuring a minimum income for farmers. finally, the report does not include any proposal for the establishment of mechanisms to deal with climate change, which directly affects european farmers.
in writing. the regulations implementing the cap "health diagnosis" are a decisive step in controlling agricultural production by the monopoly business groups, with the aim of increasing their profits, and at the same time preparing the ground for the full-scale attack on the already weakened small and medium-sized farms in 2013. large capital is pushing for greater and faster cap reforms and its adaptation to wto rules in order to concentrate even more land for multinationals, consolidate their dominance in food production and trade and strengthen their position in international competition. the cap's effects on small and medium-sized farmers are already visible, especially after the decoupling of aid from production with the 2003 revision: abandonment of crops, reduction of the rural population, clearing, desertification of the countryside, negative effects on the environment. they are also visible to workers facing the unbearable cost of rising food prices and the growing risks to public health from hazardous substances, questionable raw materials and production methods. we are radically opposed to the proposed regulations which reveal the anti-agricultural character of the cap. we call on small and mediumsized farmers to join the workers in the common struggle against the anti-agricultural policy of the eu and capital. mr president, both the proposals for directives and the two reports are implementing the european union's general immigration policy, which aims to provide cheap labour for european capital to increase its profits. the directive on the granting of a blue card for entry and work in the european union to highly skilled migrants is a brain drain on the poorer countries in order to give european monopolies a better position in global competition, particularly with the united states of america. it does not confer any substantive rights and benefits on beneficiaries, since it requires a pre-existing employment contract. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the second directive and report on the single residence and work card are moving in the same direction. only those with a job will be able to enter the european union and take leave. so immigrants are at the mercy of employers. firing will be tantamount to deportation. and for the illegal ones, there's the european immigration pact's trap of 18 months detention, deportation and a five-year ban on entry. the overall policy of the european union legitimizes the cruel and brutal exploitation of immigrants and of workers in the european union as a whole. we support the struggle of immigrants for equal labour and social rights, the struggle to defend and extend the rights of workers throughout the european union.
mr president, mr vice-president of the commission, for a decade now, virtually no real discussion has taken place about how member states can work together to make europe a more attractive destination for the legal migrants our societies need and a more humane place for those already living among us. indicative of the almost monotonous way in which europe is focusing on the police approach to migration policy is the recent "return directive", which treats, as we know, many poor migrants as common criminals. the main reason for this is that most of the member states of europe have not yet succeeded, on the one hand, in implementing effective integration programmes for immigrants and, on the other, in convincing a large part of their public that the inevitable increase in the diversity of our societies is a desirable development that promotes our economic and social development. in this context, the legislative initiatives we are discussing today can only be welcomed. it is perhaps the first serious attempt to create a common european policy on legal immigration, despite the relative timidity of some of the proposals and despite their problems, some of which we are addressing with amendments such as - many rightly said - the risk of deforestation of poor countries by the most skilled workers. at the same time, however, these individual arrangements concern a small number of privileged, one might say, legal immigrants. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one.
mr president, mr vice-president, mr president-in-office of the council, the european union is still not considered attractive to highly qualified workers from third countries, while thousands of unskilled migrants are entering the union. european migration policy therefore requires a broad and coherent overall approach to peace and security, european development policy and integration and employment policies. the legislative proposal seeks to establish common criteria for a rapid admission procedure for highly qualified migrants. it is necessary to have common, uniform definitions for access to 27 labour markets. it is widely recognised that the european union needs to be able to use skilled manpower from third countries in the long term to enhance its competitiveness and greater economic growth. but there are conditions. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. the development policy must guarantee the availability of capacity from third countries. the rapporteur - whom i am sorry to hear about - stresses that the arrival of immigrants for highly skilled work cannot be a long-term solution to economic and demographic problems, since economic migration generally affects the national labour markets of the member states. the principle of subsidiarity must be respected as long as there are no uniform social systems and uniform labour legislation. the european parliament therefore recommends that the principle of community preference be strictly observed. the member states, within the framework of their national sovereignty, must determine the volume of admission of third-country nationals and have the right to a zero quota. the granting of a blue card, even if the conditions are met, is left to the discretion of each member state. the european added value is provided by mobility after two years of legal migration to another member state.
vice-president of the commission. − the commission presented its autumn forecast on 3 november, which indicates that the economic outlook is bleak: economic growth is expected to come to a standstill in 2009, increasing by a meagre 0.2% in the european union. 2010 should see a gradual recovery for most eu economies, with growth projected at 1.1% for the eu as a whole. as a result, unemployment is expected to increase to 7.8% in the eu in 2009, with further increase projected for 2010. however, next year we expect inflation to fall back quickly to 2.4% in the eu and to decelerate further in 2010. there is no question that the challenges we face are substantial. hence the commission is now developing a comprehensive strategy to manage the financial crisis and limit the economic downturn. the basis of this strategy is set down in the communication entitled ‘from financial crisis to recovery: a european framework for action’, which indicates how the eu should tackle the next stages of the crisis in a united, coordinated manner. action should be geared towards three objectives: first, building a new financial market architecture at eu level; second, dealing with the impact on the real economy and, third, coordinating a global response to the financial crisis. on 26 november the commission will propose a more detailed version of this eu recovery plan, under the umbrella of the lisbon strategy for growth and jobs. our aim is to bring together a series of targeted short-term initiatives that will help counter adverse effects on the wider economy, while adapting the medium to long-term measures of the lisbon strategy to take account of the crisis.

member of the commission. − researchers are at the heart of knowledge creation, transfer and exploitation. they are the key for europe to turn the fifth freedom – the freedom of movement of knowledge – into reality, and with that to shape the knowledge-based economy. the supply of human resources for research is indeed best reflected in the number of new university graduates. the benchmark adopted by the education council in 2003, to increase by 15% the number of graduates in member states and decrease gender imbalance by 2010, has been reached. in 2006 there were in the eu-27 about 200 000 more mathematics, science and technology graduates than in 2000. it is clear that not all university graduates go into research. for the european union an additional factor here is that, due to the lower share of private research investments in europe compared to other continents, the market for researchers in the eu is relatively smaller than those of our competitors. on top of that, there is strong competition for attracting and keeping the most talented researchers. this is first and foremost a competition between research and other economic sectors. but there is also a competition between countries and world regions – in particular the us, but also increasingly china and india. the european union is facing the upcoming retirement of generations of researchers in europe, with no prospect of their complete replacement. the situation will get worse if young people are not attracted into the research profession. what is at stake is whether europe in the long term can remain and further develop as a world-class location for research and development. the fact is that researchers in europe are still faced with serious obstacles and a lack of opportunities. when i talk to researchers across europe, i hear about unattractive working conditions and career prospects, an often precarious status and short-term contracts. furthermore, many researchers are still trained in a way which does not equip them with the skills needed in a modern knowledge economy. there are strong disincentives for researchers wishing to move jobs within academia and industry and vice versa. finally, the structural fragmentation of the european researchers’ labour market hinders the transnational mobility of researchers within the european union, due to, in particular, a lack of open, merit-based recruitment and to cultural factors, as well as problems encountered by highly mobile workers in such fields as social security, taxation and transferability of supplementary pension rights. it is therefore high time for europe to step up its efforts to ensure the availability of the necessary researchers in the years ahead. that is precisely why the commission last may proposed a european partnership for researchers: a partnership with and among member states entailing a focused framework to make rapid progress across europe in key areas determining better careers and more mobility. the council has responded favourably to this initiative and we are about to embark on its implementation, centred on national action plans and mutual learning. evidence-based monitoring of progress, data-collection on mobility and career patterns are also foreseen. so, while we currently have very few data, the aim is to provide ourselves with the better statistics that the honourable member is looking for. we have many of the other data but not exactly these specific data. the commission communication on the european partnership for researchers is currently under consideration in this parliament. the commission looks forward to parliament’s opinion, which will hopefully reinforce this common endeavour for the future of research in europe.

president of the council. - mr president, commissioner, rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, we are here tonight to discuss a matter which has occupied us for several years, a matter which is of importance to all european workers, namely the revision of the directive on working time. the text which is being presented to the european parliament today is the result of a compromise reached in the council on 9 june last during the slovenian presidency. this compromise concerned both the working time directive and the interim work directive. the council adopted it in the belief that it represents progress for the situation of workers in europe in both its dimensions. with the temporary work directive, on the one hand, the principle of equal treatment on the first day becomes the rule in europe. this is a step forward for the millions of people who work in this sector. the european parliament adopted this directive definitively on 22 october last, and i welcome this decision which will improve the situation of temporary workers in the 17 member states where the principle of equal treatment on the first day is not provided for in national legislation. with the compromise on working time, on the other hand, we are introducing safeguards to the 1993 opt-out, which are in place without restrictions and without a time limit. the text now provides for a ceiling of 60 or 65 hours, depending on the case, compared with the previous limit of 78 hours per week. it also makes it impossible to sign an individual opt-out agreement for four weeks after the recruitment and it introduces increased control by the labour inspectorate. i would add that the council's common position introduces an explicit clause for the revision of the opt-out. finally, i would stress that the slovenian compromise allows for the specific nature of childcare to be taken into account, which will help many countries, particularly in the field of health. of course, the revision of the working time directive is a compromise and, as in all compromises, some of our initial objectives have had to be set aside. i am thinking in particular of the abolition of the opt-out which france defended with other countries, but this line was a minority one and we did not have the balance of forces to impose it on the council. when you vote on second reading, it is important that you bear in mind the objective which we must have: to reach a text acceptable to all, avoiding conciliation where possible. of course there is a significant gap between parliament's opinion at first reading and the council's common position, but parliament must consider that there is an urgency for some states to solve the problem of guard time, that the slovenian compromise contains advances for workers, and that there is no majority in the council to abolish the opt-out which has existed without limit since 1993. in the light of the debates you are about to have, i would like to draw your attention in particular to two points. the council's objective in defining the term 'time in custody' is often misunderstood. the aim is not to call into question the acquired rights of workers, but to safeguard the existing balances in certain member states. the debate in the european parliament could help to shed light on the issues involved in this new definition. the council's intention is not to organise a retreat or a regression of rights. on the contrary, it seeks to preserve the existing balances in the member states, which consist in calculating childcare time in a specific way, to take account of the periods of inactivity it involves. on the revision clause of the opt-out, we must conclude without making winners or losers because, objectively, the balance of power does not allow it. the slovenian compromise provides for the revision of the directive after an evaluation report, in six years. so everything remains open, and that is why i am calling for a truce on this opt-out issue. the european parliament is in a position of responsibility tonight. the outcome of this case, which has been open since 2004, will depend on the vote you take. i hope that the debate which is now opening will abandon any idea of confrontation and take account of the council's strong aspirations as reflected in the common position. i am convinced that in this spirit you can pave the way for a balanced solution that can be reached quickly.

the rapporteur. - the mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the new financial management rules, as laid down in general regulation 1083 of 2006, include provisions on the financial contribution from the funds, and in particular those relating to revenue-generating projects (article 55), projects which, with their clear risk of over-financing, require special treatment in order to allow revenue to be taken into account in the calculation of the largest amount of community funding. it is therefore necessary to define a method for calculating the revenue from these projects. in the previous period 2000-2006, this principle was applied in practice by a flat-rate method. the new programming period, in accordance with the commission proposal, which was accepted by the council, applies a more precise and rigorous approach to the calculation of community funding for revenue-generating projects. the new approach is based on the calculation of the maximum eligible expenditure, rather than a flat-rate reduction in the co-financing rate. according to article 55, for the period 2007-2013, a revenue-generating project is any transaction involving investment in infrastructure the use of which is subject to charges directly borne by users or any transaction involving the sale or lease of land or buildings or any other provision of services for remuneration. an important difference of the new period is that, according to the definition in the paragraph, the provisions of article 55 apply to a wide range of projects considered to generate revenue and not only to infrastructure investment projects generating significant net revenue, such as the period 2000-2006. the results of an informal consultation of the european commission with the member states have shown that the provisions of article 55 are inappropriate for projects co-financed by the european social fund, which mainly finances intangible operations rather than infrastructure projects. the same applies to small projects co-financed by the european regional development fund and the cohesion fund. for these projects, the monitoring rules to be observed, such as the fact that revenues may be taken into account even three years after the closure of the operational programme, are disproportionately bureaucratic in relation to the amounts expected and constitute a serious risk in the execution of the programmes. for this reason, and after consulting the member states, the commission considered it necessary to adopt an amendment to regulation (ec) no 1083/2006, which should be limited to article 55 (5) and concern only the following two points: the exclusion from the provisions of article 55 of operations co-financed by the european social fund and the establishment of a threshold of eur 1 million below which projects from the erdf or the cohesion fund will be excluded from the provisions of article 55 as regards the calculation of the maximum eligible expenditure and as regards monitoring. the other provisions of article 55 shall not be amended. moreover, since it is important to ensure that common rules for the implementation of projects are applied throughout the programming period, a retroactive clause has been included so that the revised provision will apply from 1 august 2006. this technical amendment will simplify the management of revenue-generating projects as much as possible by reducing the administrative burden in accordance with the principle of proportionality.

member of the commission. − madam president, today and tomorrow are one of those very rare occasions when politicians can write history. the energy and climate package that you are going to vote on tomorrow is a landmark package of legislation which is significant not only for the european union, but for the international efforts to address climate change, and will have consequences within the european union and internationally. i would like to thank the french presidency for its dedication and the work it has done to reach a compromise, but mainly i would like to express my sincere thanks and appreciation to the european parliament for the work it has done all this time, to all the political groups and to the rapporteurs. everybody has contributed constructively in bringing the compromise to the level where a vote tomorrow will be promising. i think that although a lot of concerns were expressed – there were a lot of proposals, and many of these were taken on board – and everybody is a little bit dissatisfied, this does not mean that the package is not equitable and is not ambitious. it is ambitious, equitable, fair, and it is going to deliver the environmental objective we have set by reducing by 20% the greenhouse emissions in the european union by 2020. so the architecture of the package remains as it was in our proposal and the environmental integrity of the package has been fully preserved and also the fair distribution of the efforts amongst the various parties. the package before you contains a set of measures which is the most ambitious in the world. only recently some voices around the world have claimed they would imitate our package, and this is very encouraging. the european union is leading the world as regards climate change and, by adopting this package through your vote tomorrow, we shall confirm our international role in leading the world in addressing climate change, and at the same time we shall ensure that the benefits to our countries from the early move to a low-carbon economy will indeed come. the european union is the first region in the world that has reduced emissions. we are going to deliver on our kyoto protocol targets, both as the eu-15 and as the eu-27, we are going to achieve the 8% reduction target; indeed, due to the efforts of the new member states, as the eu-27 we are even going to overshoot the 8% reduction target. we are the only region in the world where there is an emissions trading system that works well and where we have put a price on carbon. the european union is the region in the world investing most in the developing countries, in clean development projects, which are useful not only because we get credit for the investments made in those countries, but also because we reduce global greenhouse emissions and because we help in transferring technology in those developing countries, investing there and creating jobs. the european union is the region of the world that invests most heavily in research, and by our package and by the provision that mr borloo referred to previously of investing the proceeds from auctioning 300 million tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2015, which could be about eur 9 billion, we are going to invest even more in research. the european union is also the only region in the world that will have set a 20% unilateral target by adopting this package tomorrow, and our leaders have reconfirmed our 30% reduction, which is necessary in order to effectively fight climate change (according to the most recent scientific information, even this 30% will perhaps not be enough). by adopting this package tomorrow we will have made not just a step forward, but a leap forward in fighting climate change and also setting the example for other countries, other regions of the world to follow us. some have already done so. yesterday, australia announced a package to fight climate change. it is not as ambitious as ours but still very important. it has set a unilateral target, it is introducing a cap-and-trade system and it is very ambitious about the medium- and long-term targets. it has underlined its willingness to work together with us in reaching an international agreement in copenhagen. everybody now knows what president-elect obama has set as priorities – energy security, climate change – and he repeated this again yesterday. the european union is leading by producing various papers and studies, which will be very useful in our negotiations next year. it was apparent in poznań last week that the countries of the world are determined to work hard next year in order to secure an ambitious international agreement in copenhagen and the european union will contribute to this objective by producing papers on how this agreement should be, what the basic elements should be, what the structure should be and also how we can finance this agreement. when we were discussing this package, various concerns were expressed: concerns about carbon leakage, which is whether carbon-intensive industries, because of the emissions trading system and mainly because of the auctioning, will move to countries without carbon restraints and will continue emitting carbon dioxide in those countries which do not have any limitations (which will also be detrimental to the european union because we shall lose jobs). concerns were expressed by some member states which rely heavily on coal regarding auctioning in the power sector and some other countries expressed their concern regarding flexibility in the effort-sharing proposal. by the compromise reached all those concerns will be taken care of. for industry, long-term predictability has been assured and free allowances will be given and the competitiveness question will be taken care of. at the same time, it should be stressed that these industries will still make their fair contribution to reducing emissions in the european union because they are not only subject to the cap in the emissions trading system, but also they have to comply with the benchmark of best available technologies. so, even these industries are going to make reductions. let me turn to auctioning in the energy sector, because i have heard a lot of complaints and dissatisfaction that we have allowed some member states an opt-out regarding this sector. firstly, it should be underlined that this is an option for the member states because they were very concerned about the social impact of our proposal. we should listen to those concerns, and we did listen. however, in my opinion, when the time comes they will not use this opt-out for the simple reason – especially for those countries in which the energy sector is privately owned and prices are unregulated – that they will have the dilemma of whether to give the money to the finance ministry – to the state – to be used for good causes or to permit the private sector to make windfall profits, profits without any reason. this is something we shall see; it could become a political question in the future. so, i would say to those who object to our agreement on this particular point that they have the possibility in their own countries to persuade their governments not to exercise this option when the time comes. at the same time, if those member states consider that it is important for social or other reasons to use this opt-out, they are able to do so. concerning flexibility on the cdms and the effort-sharing there: firstly, there are many numbers floating around at the moment as to how much of the effort of reducing emissions will be done domestically and how much will be permitted to be done abroad. i should underline that all these comparisons refer to 2005. the actual reductions which should be carried out domestically are much larger, because they should be compared to 2020 and to the business as usual. the actual reductions will be much larger in the european union. i have asked my services to provide me with an analysis and for the total effort-sharing and ets the efforts within the european union will be about 60%; 41% could be abroad, in developing countries. let us not forget that we need investment in developing countries. this is one of those issues that are being brought up all the time by our international partners and also here in the european union by all those who are interested in transferring technology and making investments and reducing carbon dioxide emissions in developing countries. why is it bad? we must have a balance, because otherwise, if we make too much effort abroad and not domestically, it would mean that all the benefits for our business and industry in the european union would be lost, because our package is not only about fighting climate change but also about creating a more efficient economy. we are going to provide the incentives to make our business and industry more resource- and energy-efficient, and an energy-efficient, resource-efficient business means an economically efficient business – a more competitive business – which, in turn, means innovation in the european union. so we do need more effort in the european union. this is something that we should try to do. again, for all those who are complaining about this point of compromise, there is a great possibility: go to your countries and ask the governments of austria, sweden, denmark, finland and the other countries – there are 12 of them listed – which have asked for this one additional per cent, and tell them not to use the cdms that are permitted under this compromise. it is up to you. do it there, not here. here you should vote for the package. the package comes together: it is not one proposal here and one proposal there; one affects the other. so, do not make the mistake. if you have objections, do it in your countries, do it in the countries that have this possibility to get the one per cent additional cdm. i am not going to speak about the fourth concern, which was solidarity. mr borloo gave the answer and the solution reached by the french presidency was very wise. i do not want to take up any more time, because i have already spoken too much. what is important now is to look forward. we should look to copenhagen. we have a year of tough negotiations ahead of us. let us work together again – the european parliament, the council and the commission – in order to persuade our international partners to reach an agreement in copenhagen. thirty per cent is the minimum that we have to agree in copenhagen in order to fight climate change effectively. we should start working now. at the same time, we have to continue to take care of our industries. coming back to the question of carbon liquids, this is not only a question of preserving our jobs, employment and competitiveness, but also an environmental question. i do not want to see companies reallocating and emitting in countries without carbon constraints. so it is an environmental, a social and an economic issue, and our compromise balances all those issues: the social issues, the economic issues and the environmental issues. i think that we should continue on this path. in implementing this package, we should also continue our cooperation, of course with the council, of course with the european parliament, but also let us bring the social partners into this discussion. we should work together because this is very important for europe; it is very important for the world. member of the commission. - mr mitchell, price stability is defined in the treaty as the main mandate. the first mandate of the european central bank is to preserve price stability. once that mandate, that main objective, is achieved, or to the extent that it is achieved, the mandate is for monetary policy to cooperate with the other objectives of economic policy. the bank itself and the other european institutions must adhere to this. what does the bank mean by price stability? i think he defined it very clearly from 2003 - if i remember correctly - as inflation below 2% but very close to 2% in the medium term. for all previous years since 1999 until now, approaching this target of below 2% but close to 2% tended to reduce inflation. next year - if the forecasts are confirmed - price stability may be interpreted as approaching 2% without going over 2% for the first time, because we will probably be living in a situation where not only month-on-month inflation but perhaps the medium-term inflation expectations themselves are below 2%. but the mandate remains the same. the instruments and the way of approaching the objective will be different, of course, but that will still be the objective. the second area of activity or second block of activities of the bank, which is extremely important at the moment - of any central bank, but certainly of the european central bank - is to provide liquidity. i think the bank is doing what it should be doing, but nobody is hiding from it - and the bank says it very clearly - that it provides liquidity in the morning but, normally, before closing the window late in the afternoon, it receives liquidity from financial institutions that have not used that liquidity for their credit functions. and there is a discussion that is open: in the newspapers these days there are statements by the bank's vice-president, mr papademos, and some other officials announcing that the bank is discussing how it should use the necessary instruments to make this provision of liquidity effective and not just a circle that ends in the afternoon by returning the money to the place where the money left in the morning. as regards the second question, on the difference: in some of the countries which are members of the european union and not members of the euro area, inflation is higher than that of the vast majority of the countries in the euro area. if you look at the note distributed by eurostat this morning on inflation at the end of november, you will see that there are a majority of countries in the european union outside the euro area that have an inflation rate higher than the country with the highest inflation in the euro area. so, right now, outside the euro area there is more inflation, largely because outside the euro area there are countries in a process of rapid convergence and where a series of effects of higher intensity in energy use, of greater external dependence on energy that has increased in price or of the 'balassa-samuelson effect', said in technical jargon, leads to greater inflationary pressure. and by sector, inflation is clearly higher in the services sector. despite this fall in year-on-year inflation, which has been very rapid in recent months, you will see that inflation in the services sector has remained virtually constant (2.5-2.6%); inflation in foodstuffs or food processed products or industrial goods has fluctuated much more as a result of the reasons i have mentioned in my reply to mr medina ortega, but the services sector has maintained an inflation rate that is above the price stability objective, which is to remain below 2%. nevertheless, this inflation rate is close to 2%.

member of the commission. - madam president, as the commission has repeatedly pointed out, a rule prohibiting pharmacists established in one member state from accepting a prescription for personal use from a doctor established in another member state goes beyond the necessary arrangements designed to protect public health and is therefore contrary to community law, in particular article 49 of the treaty. consequently, if a medicinal product is authorised in the territory of a member state pursuant to article 6 (1) of directive 2001/83, that member state must ensure that prescriptions issued by authorised persons in other member states may be used in its territory. in accordance with the case law of the european court of justice, any restriction on such recognition must be non-discriminatory, justified and proportionate. furthermore, the commission considers that it would be proportionate for reasons of public health for national legislation to provide that the pharmacist may refuse to execute a prescription if there are legitimate and justified doubts as to the authenticity of the prescription, and to exclude medicinal products for which special medical prescriptions are required as provided for in article 71 (2) of directive 2001/83. as regards article 14 of the proposed directive on the application of patients' rights to crossborder healthcare, this aims to ensure the recognition of prescriptions lawfully issued in another member state within the limits i have mentioned above. the purpose of article 14 (2) is to facilitate the implementation of the recognition of prescriptions issued in another member state by adopting measures to assist pharmacists in executing prescriptions issued in another member state without the slightest doubt as to the authenticity of the prescription or the correct identification of the prescribed medicinal product. the commission cannot give details of the measures to be adopted under article 14 because these measures will naturally be adopted in accordance with the regulatory procedure in a committee composed of representatives of the member states, so the commission cannot foresee at this stage which measures will be decided by the representatives of the member states. the commission would also point out that article 14 (2) merely refers to measures to ensure the correct identification of prescribed medicinal products and does not provide for any specific solution to achieve this objective. the commission is also aware of the point raised by the honourable member of the european parliament concerning the different policies followed in the various member states as regards the possibility of replacing a medicinal product which is perhaps issued in the original form by another medicinal product which is a generic product, but this issue is being addressed by the member states themselves. the commission cannot force member states to decide whether pharmacists can substitute one medicine for another. this is of course a matter for the member states. i should therefore like to conclude by stating that a prescription issued by a doctor established in another member state provides the same guarantees for patients as a prescription issued by a doctor established in the member state concerned and, in accordance with the judgments of the court of justice of 7 march in schumacher and in commission v germany in 1990, the same applies to medicinal products purchased from pharmacists in other member states.
